quotes.text: Joel favored tightly structured pop melodies and down-to-earth songwriting.

When I first listened to The Stranger, what I loved most was Billy's piano. It wasn't so much his technique or the nimbleness of his fingers—he's a damned fine pianist—but the beautiful clarity that came out through my headphones.

Billy wanted to record with his touring band because they brought more life to the party but Martin heard their rougher sound as a detriment and wanted to use session players instead—you know, the guys who are "not paid to think, just play" in Ray Davies' memorable condemnation. Billy put his foot down, waved goodbye to George Martin and made one of the best decisions of his life by hiring Phil Ramone to produce The Stranger—and Billy's next five albums.
I've discussed before at length how much I'm impressed at the way he intentionally stopped releasing albums back in 1993 when he didn't feel like he had any more good songs in him.
Billy Joel's musical legacy would be remembered much differently had he continued cranking out rote, bland albums after River of Dreams like so many of his contemporaries did.

In 1983 those artists still left standing after the 70s slouched to an end faced a radically changed musical landscape. The ground had shifted under their feet, and some of them reacted by attempting to embrace musical trends that suited them poorly.

While everyone else was trying to embrace musical trends they didn't understand and had little aptitude for anyway, Billy Joel did the most unexpected thing possible – he released a throwback album that didn't bother being the least bit contemporary or modern. An album full of songs clearly inspired by those released twenty or more years earlier.

Billy Joel resisted the temptation almost all popular artists at the time succumbed to – even the generally trend-proof Robert Plant released Shaken 'n' Stirred in that period, and it speaks to how ubiquitous it was for popular artists from the 70s to be flailing around in the 80s in a vain and desperate attempt to fit in with the sounds that ruled the charts at the time.

The structures of the songs more or less reflect the structures of an earlier age, and in that sense Joel and producer Phil Ramone deserve a tremendous amount of credit. Joel crafted the songs and Ramone crafted the arrangements in way that were true to music that inspired them.

One thing that strikes me about the album – other than the somewhat disturbing cover – is that considering this is Billy Joel, how many of the songs aren't built around piano parts. "Piano Man" is, obviously, and "If I Only Had the Words" is, and the piano drives "The Ballad of Billy the Kid", and several others. But album opener, "Travelin' Prayer", begins with just drums. Piano comes for a minute not long after, but is conspicuously absent from the rest of the song other than a fantastic piano solo. Around the second verse a banjo kicks in, and some hoe-down fiddle playin' mosies along after a bit.

Billy Joel — whose sizable catalogue includes an apocalyptic anthem of New York, a hit accounting of history from the Truman administration to the 1980s Cola Wars and countless fawning and fatalistic ballads inspired by women who left him — is another sort of prophet.

When Joel was at his peak, producing chart-topping, traditional standards in the heyday of punk, music critics savaged him. As he started swapping genres — guitar-forward rock, doo-wop, even gospel — he was dismissed as a pasticheur, dabbling in too many styles to have any authenticity of his own.
Without a unified sound, there emerged instead a thematic thrust. As Chuck Klosterman wrote, Joel "musically amplifies mainstream depression," even if "he never tried to invent a new way to be sad."
His first producer ruined his debut album, Cold Spring Harbor, speeding up the tape and making Joel's audio sound like a chipmunk.
He knows he sounded ungrateful, riding the success of "Piano Man" and turning around with the music industry takedown "The Entertainer."
Joel has a self-destructive bent. His struggles with mental health, like his musical talent, were inherited.
